name: Belgium
summary_text: Belgium is a top-tier destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender and name change by self-declaration has been available since 2018, anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and expression across employment, housing and services, hate crime and hate speech are both criminalised for gender identity, and transphobia is a separately tracked hate-crime motive. Belgium also passed Europe's first femicide law (2023), with protections for gender minorities. The framework is politically stable with no rollback movement — a contrast with several neighbours (the UK's in-force facilities code, Portugal's first-reading repeal attempt, Germany's repeal review). The main caveat is a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ violence and intimidation: the equality body Unia reported in 2025 that gay men and transgender people are increasingly targeted, and an RTBF investigation documented dating-app ambush attacks on queer men in urban nightlife. For a visitor this is a comfortable environment with the usual urban-nightlife caution: zero legal exposure, functioning institutions, and a welcoming day-to-day climate, particularly in Brussels.

sources.title: Belgium | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Belgium has robust protections - discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of SOGISC banned; same-sex marriage and adoption; legal name and gender-marker change based on self-determination. Europe's first femicide law (2023) covers all gender-based homicide; a 2023 law bans conversion practices. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, though a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for nonconsensual interventions.

sources.title: Belgium - Rainbow Map
sources.claim_summary: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Belgium: overall index score and per-category compliance breakdown (legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality & non-discrimination, family, civil society, asylum, intersex).

sources.title: LGBTQI+ people increasingly the target of violence and intimidation | VRT NWS: news
sources.claim_summary: VRT NWS (May 2025): despite Belgium's progressive reputation, equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men report rising violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases handled by Unia in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is 'dating app traps' - gay men lured via apps, ambushed, beaten and robbed; a high-profile case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025.

sources.title: Stay safe: RTBF investigation reveals rising homophobic attacks in Belgium -
sources.claim_summary: KET Magazine (Feb 2025) summarising an RTBF investigation into rising homophobic attacks in Belgium orchestrated through dating apps: perpetrators use fake profiles to arrange meetings, then ambush victims in isolated locations where they are robbed, humiliated or assaulted. Police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported due to fear or shame.

sources.title: National frameworks to address hate crime in Belgium | HCRW
sources.claim_summary: OSCE/ODIHR page on Belgium's national hate-crime frameworks: hate crimes are not defined in Belgian legislation and no code exists to record them as such; violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions instead.

sources.title: Gender self-identification | Brussels-Capital Region
sources.claim_summary: Official Brussels-Capital Region page on changing gender registration on ID cards: free of charge, 3-6 weeks processing, requires a valid identity document, a medical certificate attesting to sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision; application made in person at the commune, digital mode available.

sources.title: New legislation for transgender persons | Justice
sources.claim_summary: Belgian Federal Justice Department page: since 1 January 2018 (Law of 25 June 2017), trans people can change registered gender and first names without medical conditions, via a declaration to the civil registrar. On 19 June 2019 the Constitutional Court partially annulled the law; pending new provisions, applications continue under the current procedure.

sources.title: LGBTQIA+ travel in Belgium | Intrepid Travel US
sources.claim_summary: Intrepid Travel country guide: Belgium is 'one of the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers in the world', with forward-thinking attitudes and thriving queer culture in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège.

sources.title: LGBT+ Rights in Belgium – A Short Guide
sources.claim_summary: Discovering Belgium guide (2024): overview of LGBT+ rights history and current status - sex between men decriminalised as far back as 1795 under the French penal code, though public-indecency laws and police harassment persisted; covers key figures, organisations, current rights, and where to report homophobia.

'Being transgender in Belgium - Ten years later' (2017), by Motmans, Wyverkens, Defreyne et al. for the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men: a large survey study of trans people in Belgium covering gender identity, coming out, openness, obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed per experienced gender, official name/gender registration change, work, sex work, economic status and well-being.

sources.title: Zelfbeschikking centraal in nieuwe transgenderwet | Oud-Minister en ere-volksvertegenwoordiger
sources.claim_summary: Press release (May 2017, in Dutch) from Justice Minister Koen Geens on Belgium's new transgender law: self-determination is the starting point - legal gender change via a purely administrative procedure with all medical conditions (including sterilisation/surgery) scrapped; includes a reflection period and public-order safeguards; notes name-change requests rose from 85 (2012) to 187 (2016).
